title: Make simple decisions about earning, spending, saving and giving

lesson.title: Earn It, Then Give It a Job

steps.say: You already know how to add up what things cost, like adding a bag of apples and a pack of pencils to get a total. Today we use that same adding skill for something new: when you earn some money, you decide how much to spend, how much to save, and how much to give.

Here is the big idea. Every dollar you earn gets a job. Some dollars have the job of spending, some have the job of saving, and some have the job of giving. Say you earn twenty dollars shovelling snow. You could give eight dollars the spend job, eight dollars the save job, and four dollars the give job. Add them up: eight plus eight plus four is twenty. Perfect, every dollar has a job and nothing is left over.

visual.caption: Twenty dollars earned, split into three jobs

steps.say: Now let's plan together. Priya walks dogs in her Kelowna neighbourhood and earns twenty-four dollars. She wants a book that costs ten dollars, she is saving up for a soccer ball, and she likes helping the animal shelter. Her plan is: spend ten dollars, save ten dollars, give four dollars. Let's check it the way we check a shopping total. Ten plus ten is twenty, and twenty plus four is twenty-four. It fits exactly. Priya's plan works.

visual.caption: Priya's plan adds up to exactly twenty-four dollars

steps.say: Here is the mistake lots of kids make. Priya sees a bigger book for fifteen dollars and thinks, I will just buy that one instead, and keep everything else the same. So her plan becomes: spend fifteen, save ten, give four. Let's add. Fifteen plus ten is twenty-five, and twenty-five plus four is twenty-nine. But she only earned twenty-four dollars! Twenty-nine is five dollars more than twenty-four, so those last five dollars simply do not exist. The plan does not fit.

visual.caption: Twenty-nine dollars planned, but only twenty-four earned

steps.say: So Priya fixes it. If she really wants the fifteen dollar book, she has to take those five dollars from another job. She saves five dollars instead of ten, and still gives four. Fifteen plus five is twenty, plus four is twenty-four. It fits again. That is the real decision: when you spend more on one thing, something else gets less.

visual.caption: The fixed plan: still twenty-four dollars in total

steps.say: So remember: add up your spend, save, and give amounts, and the total must not be bigger than the money you actually earned.

lesson.answer: Spend plus save plus give must add up to the money you earned — never more.

practice.question: Owen earns twenty-eight dollars raking leaves for a neighbour in Victoria. He plans to spend fourteen dollars on a comic book, save ten dollars for a bike helmet, and give six dollars to the food bank. Add up his plan. Does it fit the twenty-eight dollars he earned? If not, by how much is he over, and name one way he could fix it.
practice.answer: Fourteen plus ten plus six is thirty dollars. That is two dollars more than the twenty-eight he earned, so the plan does not fit. He is over by two dollars. He could fix it by spending twelve dollars instead of fourteen (twelve plus ten plus six is twenty-eight), or by saving only eight dollars.
